assessment.instructions: You may consult Blackburn's Chapter 5 and the accompanying LLM-Wiki note. Answer all questions. For multiple-choice questions, select the single best answer. For short answers, prioritize precise argument reconstruction over breadth. For the final prompt, state a defensible thesis and address at least one objection or limitation.

questions.prompt: What is Blackburn's preferred diagnosis of the ontological argument's central defect?

options.text: Its conclusion is probabilistic even though its premises are deductive.
It equivocates when comparing an object in reality with an object as represented in conception.
It assumes without argument that every event has a prior physical cause.
It proves only that God is morally perfect, not that God is omnipotent.

questions.prompt: Why does Blackburn regard Russell's quick objection to the first-cause argument as “a little glib”?

options.text: The theologian distinguishes dependent physical things from the allegedly self-sufficient being introduced to explain them.
Russell mistakenly treats the argument as a posteriori rather than a priori.
An infinite causal regress is formally contradictory.
Hume had already demonstrated that the material cosmos cannot be necessary.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion most accurately represents what Philo thinks the design argument could establish after its strongest concessions?

options.text: The universe was made by one omnipotent and perfectly good person.
Biological adaptation makes any inference from order irrational.
The cause or causes of order may bear some remote analogy to intelligence, without supporting richer theology.
The universe is more probably a literal organism than a designed machine.

questions.prompt: What is the primary force of the neglected-dormitory analogy in the discussion of evil?

options.text: Any suffering is deductively inconsistent with every possible deity.
Poor conditions are evidence against inferring management that is simultaneously fully informed, perfectly caring, and unlimited in power.
Human freedom explains all apparently defective conditions.
Suffering proves that the universe has multiple designers.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures Hume's maxim concerning testimony for miracles as Blackburn presents it?

options.text: Testimony is irrelevant whenever an event conflicts with a law of nature.
A miracle should be accepted whenever several sincere witnesses agree.
Testimony can support a miracle only when its falsehood would be still more extraordinary, after weighing the competing evidential forces.
Miracles are metaphysically impossible, so reports of them are necessarily false.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Cleanthes' design argument as an argument by analogy, then state two distinct objections Philo raises against the inference. Your answer should distinguish a criticism of the analogy's evidential basis from a criticism of how much theology its conclusion could support.

Explain the dilemma Blackburn sees in Demea's appeal to an incomprehensible divine nature as a response to evil. Why can this strategy preserve compatibility while making religious belief practically “inert”?

A person says: “I admit that reason and evidence do not identify which religion is true. Still, believing is rational because one possible deity offers infinite reward for faith, while disbelief offers no comparable benefit.” Evaluate this argument using Blackburn's treatment of Pascal's wager. State a thesis, reconstruct the wager's practical logic, present Blackburn's strongest objection, and explain whether that objection shows that religious belief is false or only that this prudential argument fails.

q1.explanation: Blackburn's diagnosis is the equivocation between an object in reality and an object as represented in conception: the imagined turkey shows that an imagined object is not a deficient real object available for cross-domain comparison, and a maximally specified concept does not secure a referent.

q2.explanation: Blackburn calls the objection a little glib because the theologian applies dependency to ordinary physical things and then introduces a categorically self-sufficient terminus; Russell's “everything whatsoever has a distinct previous cause” does not by itself catch a formal contradiction.

q3.explanation: Philo allows at most that the cause or causes of order bear a remote and undefined analogy to human intelligence — which does not establish unity, omnipotence, goodness, personality or practical authority.

q4.explanation: The analogy is evidential rather than a universal deductive disproof: given observable misery one would not infer management that is simultaneously fully informed, perfectly caring and unlimited in corrective resources, which presses directly on Cleanthes' inference from the world to the creator's attributes.

q5.explanation: Hume requires weighing the probability of testimonial failure against the probability of the reported event: testimony commands belief only if its falsehood would be more extraordinary than the miracle, with residual confidence proportioned to the evidential balance. He need not declare miracles metaphysically impossible.

locators.note: The key cites 2290–2324 and 2358–2360; this locator carries the wider of the two ranges.

q6.reference_answer: Cleanthes argues that nature's adjustment of means to ends resembles human artefacts; since similar effects probably have similar causes and artefacts arise from intelligence, nature probably has an intelligent cause. Philo first challenges the evidential basis: the universe and artefacts are not sufficiently similar, and we have no experience of universe production that would calibrate the causal analogy. Second, even if something like design were granted, it radically underdetermines theology: it could involve many designers, a defective or dependent designer, or only a remote analogy to intelligence, not the single perfect God of classical theism.

criteria.description: Full credit: states Cleanthes' argument as an argument by analogy, naming both analogues — the adjustment of means to ends in nature and in human artefacts — and the principle that like effects are presumed to have like causes. The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 4 points.

Full credit: draws the inference the analogy is meant to license — that the cause of nature's order is an intelligent cosmic cause, proportioned to the effect. The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 4 points.

Full credit: gives Philo's objection to the analogy's evidential basis, with a reason why the inference fails — insufficient similarity between universe and artefact, no experience of universe production to calibrate the causal analogy, or competing natural analogies (generation, vegetation) that fit as well. Naming the disanalogy without a reason why it defeats the inference earns half. The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 4 points.

Full credit: gives Philo's scope objection — that even a granted design conclusion underdetermines theology, supporting at most an undefined, possibly multiple, possibly defective cause rather than one perfect, omnipotent, benevolent deity. The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 4 points.

q7.reference_answer: Demea can say that apparently gratuitous suffering is compatible with God because divine goodness and purposes are beyond human understanding. This blocks an inference from human standards of goodness to a contradiction. But if divine goodness has no usable relation to human goodness, belief in it yields no expectations about suffering and no guidance about conduct. An undefined cause remotely analogous to intelligence becomes indistinguishable in practice from no explanatory posit at all: it is protected from refutation by losing content.

criteria.description: Full credit: distinguishes Demea's move from Cleanthes' — Demea does not infer God's attributes from the world's apparent quality, so the evidential problem does not reach him in the same way. The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 4 points.

Full credit: explains that an incomprehensible divine nature preserves bare compatibility with evil, because human standards of goodness cannot be used to derive a contradiction. The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 4 points.

Full credit: explains that removing ordinary content from “goodness” removes predictions about how the world will go and moral guidance about conduct — the word no longer constrains anything. The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 4 points.

Full credit: states the tradeoff explicitly — that immunity from refutation is purchased by explanatory and practical inertness, so the posit approaches indistinguishability from no posit at all. Naming inertness without stating what it costs earns half. The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 4 points.

q8.reference_answer: A strong answer should argue that Blackburn's false-options objection defeats the wager as presented because metaphysical ignorance cannot justify its selective payoff matrix. This does not establish that God does not exist; it shows that the proposed prudential route to belief lacks a warranted decision model.

criteria.description: Full credit: a clear, defensible thesis that the wager fails as a prudential argument (not that theism is false). The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 7 points.

Full credit: an accurate reconstruction of the wager's practical logic — a forced practical choice, infinite payoff against negligible finite cost, and the cultivation of belief as the practical route. The key weights this element at 2 of the question's 7 points; a reconstruction missing one of these elements earns at most half.

Full credit: Blackburn's false-options objection — possible deities and religions assign different rewards and punishments, so a table of the same shape can be built for any candidate, including one that rewards evidence-sensitive non-belief. The key weights this element at 2 of the question's 7 points.

Full credit: explains why the stipulated ignorance cannot both motivate the wager and warrant its specifically Christian or monotheistic payoff assignments. Stating the point only implicitly earns half. The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 7 points.

Full credit: distinguishes the failure of the wager from a proof of atheism — the objection is to the argument's form, not to the truth of theism. The key weights this element at 1 of the question's 7 points.
